content: The Prevention of Parent-to-Child Transmission (PPTCT) program is designed to prevent the transmission of HIV from parents to their children. The system is intended to be expanded to monitor all individuals diagnosed with HIV across more than 20,000 HIV counseling and testing centers. These centers may be facility-based or standalone Integrated Counseling and Testing Centers (ICTCs). Each individual diagnosed with HIV is assigned a unique identifier, which includes the state code (2 digits), district code (3 digits), center code (3 digits), year of diagnosis (2 digits), and a sample number (5 digits). The Patient ART Linkage System (PALS) is a tool developed to track individuals diagnosed with HIV from the point of diagnosis through their linkage to care and initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) at ART centers. This system has the potential to integrate with the Inventory Management System (IMS) at ART centers, enabling the tracking of patient retention and viral load monitoring. It is anticipated that PALS will become a critical component of India’s National AIDS Control Programme, supporting the country’s efforts to achieve the goal of ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. Counselors at ICTCs are responsible for entering demographic and testing data into the PALS system. They also input data related to treatment uptake. The system allows for the monitoring of patient visits to ICTCs and ART centers, as well as referrals to ART centers for individuals who test positive for HIV. Data collected through PALS is monitored at the national level to ensure comprehensive tracking and management of HIV care and treatment. The ART coverage indicator measures the percentage of people living with HIV who are receiving antiretroviral therapy. This cross-sectional indicator provides insights into the scope of ART programs, helping program managers allocate resources such as healthcare workers and antiretroviral drugs to sustain coverage. Policymakers can use this data to advocate for the resources needed to provide lifelong ART to current and future patients. As the treat all recommendations are implemented, an increase in ART coverage is expected. However, this may also lead to increased demands on services required for initiating ART, such as HIV confirmation, baseline clinical and laboratory assessments, ARV supply, adherence preparation, and more frequent clinical consultations during the initial stages. ART coverage is a critical step in achieving universal access to lifelong treatment and is aligned with the global goal of ending the AIDS epidemic. Increasing ART coverage has been associated with reductions in tuberculosis case notifications and mortality. Facilities may aggregate data quarterly but report annually to the national level. It is essential to ensure that all patients, including those monitored by community-based health workers, are included in the facility-based ART register for accurate reporting. The system also emphasizes the importance of viral suppression as a key indicator of treatment success. Viral suppression is monitored to ensure that patients on ART achieve and maintain undetectable viral loads, which is essential for improving health outcomes and reducing HIV transmission.
